text:
This section examines Experiment A —
Historical reproduction from first

principles. Keep two questions separate:
does changing the order change

the measured outcome, and does the
proposed search method beat

a matched alternative at the same
distinct-evaluation budget? Question: do

the original five benchmark headlines
reproduce from a clean environment?

Setup: XOR, OR, AND, 3-bit parity, and
polynomial regression; seed

42; 150 generations; population 20;
tournament 3; mutation probability 0.05;

elitism 1; CPU environment. Result:
classification accuracy reached 1.0000

on XOR, OR, AND, and parity; polynomial
MSE was 0.0070

versus the earlier 0.0068. Corrections:
order mattered on four of

five tasks; AND had essentially zero
variance; repeated noisy maximum

fitness biased the historical best-ever
value upward; only positions zero

through two were functional. Visual: first
show green reproduced checks,

then reveal three amber correction cards.
Narration must say reproduction

preserved the numeric headlines but
narrowed their interpretation. Now read

evidence panel A-validation. The axes,
units, and sample are stated

on screen. The sample represented here is
the sample reported

in the source. Raw observations remain
visible wherever the artifact

provides them. Censored observations stay
marked at the cap rather

than becoming invented hitting times, and
sampled landscapes leave

unobserved permutations blank. The
supported finding is: Result:

classification accuracy reached 1.0000 on
XOR, OR, AND, and parity;

polynomial MSE was 0.0070 versus the
earlier 0.0068. The broader

claim not established here is:
Corrections: order mattered on four

of five tasks; AND had essentially zero
variance; repeated noisy

maximum fitness biased the historical
best-ever value upward; only positions

zero through two were functional. This
evidence changed the program

as follows: Carry this constraint into the
next experiment and

compare methods at equal cost. The
distinction is part of

the result. A large ordering effect does
not automatically imply

an evolutionary-search advantage, and
almost-sure convergence does not
promise practical efficiency.
